stem.text: State the sum of the series z + z2 + z3 + ... + zn, for z ≠ 1.

explanation.text: This is the standard finite geometric series sum, z + z² + ... + zⁿ = z(1 + z + ... + z^{n-1}) = z(zⁿ–1)/(z–1), using the formula for a geometric series with first term z, common ratio z, and n terms.

reasoningChain: Recognise the series as geometric with first term z, common ratio z, and n terms.
Apply the geometric series sum formula a(r^n–1)/(r–1) with a=r=z.

inferredMistakes.text: Using n+1 terms instead of n (i.e. including a z⁰=1 term that isn't actually present in the series z+z²+...+zⁿ), giving an off-by-one error in the formula.

stem.text: Find all roots of the equation 1 + z + z2 + ... + z6 = 0 in the form eiqπ, where q is rational.

points.text: ei(2k/7)π, k = 2,...,6; five other roots. No repeats or incorrect roots, z=1 must be omitted

explanation.text: 1+z+z²+...+z⁶ = (z⁷–1)/(z–1), so the equation 1+z+...+z⁶=0 (with z≠1) is equivalent to z⁷=1 with z≠1 — i.e. all the 7th roots of unity except z=1 itself. These are evenly spaced around the unit circle at angles 2kπ/7 for k=1,...,6.

reasoningChain: Rewrite 1+z+...+z⁶ as (z⁷–1)/(z–1) using the geometric series sum formula (with n=6, giving z⁷ in the numerator).
Setting this to 0 (with z≠1, so the denominator isn't zero) is equivalent to z⁷=1.
Find all 7 solutions of z⁷=1: z = e^{i2kπ/7} for k=0,1,...,6.
Exclude k=0 (which gives z=1, excluded by the original z≠1 condition), leaving the 6 roots for k=1,...,6.

inferredMistakes.text: Including k=0 (z=1) as one of the six roots, forgetting that z=1 must be excluded since it would make the original series equation trivially sum to 7, not 0, and more fundamentally the problem specifies z≠1.

stem.text: Given instead that z = e–1+iθ, use de Moivre's theorem to show that

points.text: ∑m=1∞ zm = z/(1–z) = e–1+iθ/(1–e–1+iθ); applies sum to infinity and substitutes for z. Expect eiθ/(e–eiθ)
Re(∑m=1∞ zm) = (e–1cosθ–e–2) / (1–2e–1cosθ+e–2) = (ecosθ–1)/(e2–2ecosθ+1); takes the real part, AG

markScheme.note: MS gives an alternative route substituting z = e^{iθ}/e = (cosθ+isinθ)/e directly rather than e^{-1+iθ}; both reach the same result and are worth full marks.

explanation.text: e^{-m+imθ} = (e^{-1+iθ})^m = z^m, so ∑e^{-m}cos mθ is the real part of ∑z^m with z = e^{-1+iθ}. Since |z| = e^{-1} < 1, the infinite geometric series ∑_{m=1}^∞ z^m converges to z/(1-z), and the real part of that closed form is exactly what's needed.

Taking the real part at the very end (rather than trying to separate real and imaginary parts term-by-term in the sum) is the key trick: de Moivre's theorem lets z^m = e^{-m}(cos mθ + i sin mθ), so Re(z^m) = e^{-m}cos mθ, matching the series term-by-term, and real parts add.

reasoningChain: Recognise e^{-m}cos mθ as the real part of z^m where z=e^{-1+iθ}, by de Moivre's theorem.
Sum the infinite geometric series ∑z^m (|z|<1 since |z|=e^{-1}) to get z/(1-z).
Substitute z=e^{-1+iθ} and rationalise the denominator by multiplying by the complex conjugate.
Use e^{iθ}+e^{-iθ}=2cosθ to simplify the denominator into a real expression.
Take the real part of the resulting complex fraction to isolate the answer, since Re(∑z^m)=∑Re(z^m)=∑e^{-m}cosmθ.

inferredMistakes.text: Trying to split z^m into real and imaginary parts before summing, rather than summing the geometric series as a whole first and taking the real part only at the end — this makes the algebra much harder to manage.
Forgetting to rationalise the denominator (leaving a complex number in the denominator), which makes it impossible to correctly identify the real part of the final expression.
